implementation_notes: JavaScript has no threads inside an agent, so the pattern survives only where a server handles concurrent requests on one event loop, and there Node provides AsyncLocalStorage: the documentation describes it as similar to thread-local storage in other languages, but the store is bound to the asynchronous execution chain instead of to a thread. The classic key/collection/proxy structure is replaced by a single store object - run(store, callback) establishes the value for the callback and everything it schedules, getStore() reads it anywhere downstream, and work started outside the run tree does not see it. worker_threads are the one place with real threads, and they are separate realms rather than a shared store: each worker has its own AsyncLocalStorage instances and its own module state, so context crosses the boundary as a message that the worker re-enters.
pitfalls: enterWith() is not scoped: the documentation warns that the transition continues for the entire synchronous execution and persists into later asynchronous calls, so unrelated handlers can observe the store - prefer run() per request.

Work that leaves the async chain loses the store: fire-and-forget promises, listeners registered elsewhere and callbacks from a shared pool need AsyncResource.bind or an explicit value, and getStore() returns undefined rather than failing.

Worker threads and cluster workers do not share a store: each thread has its own AsyncLocalStorage instances, so the context must travel through postMessage and be re-entered with run() inside the worker.
The store is a plain object reference: mutating it affects every reader on the same chain (there is no immutable rebinding), and keeping it in a long-lived cache keeps the whole request graph alive.
